## How This Relates to IFS

Richard Schwartz, who developed Internal Family Systems (IFS), called one of his books [No Bad Parts](https://ifs-institute.com/store/no-bad-parts), and that title is a lot of the overlap right there. In IFS even the protective parts mean well, so they get approached without shame or a fight, and "meet the protector first" would fit right in.

My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. The IFS Institute's [outline of the model](https://ifs-institute.com/resources/articles/internal-family-systems-model-outline) says "everyone has a Self," and that the Self "can and should lead," once your parts stop "blending" with it. I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru. That's still one grown-up with three jobs, like back in The Chicken-and-Egg Problem.

I have no use for another neo-Advaita, [spiritual-bypassing](https://goenka.u-dont-exist.com/) claim that a perfect Higher Self is already waiting underneath everything. A grown-up you can trust gets built through care and boundaries, and through action and direction. So what if you go looking for that calm Self and find nobody home? That's what borrowing's for. Maybe a friend plays Protector for a night, or the phone gets to ring when you know how that call goes, like back in The Parent You Inherited. One grown-up job at a time, until it's yours.

IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition. Then there's "unburdening," where the outline says parts can be helped to drop their burdens and "return to their natural balance," often after you've witnessed a part's origin story. That can be powerful. It can also get dramatic, with a lot of focus on memories and plenty of room for suggestion, and that can knock people off balance, especially if they tend to dissociate (DID-like fragmentation included) or to spiritually bypass.

And the map? It keeps expanding: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... That's a lot of rooms to get lost in. Some practitioners use the model gently. Others seem to leave people more fragmented while trying to fix the fragmenting. And having institutes and certifications behind a framework doesn't make it any truer, or safer for that matter.

Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of IFS and reparenting. Could an IFS therapist help? They may, if they're skilled and grounded. You'd want one who's trauma-informed and doesn't put ideas in your head, especially one who understands dissociation. For your little one's pain, or for shame, a good reparenting therapist may fit better. The same goes for attachment wounds or abandoning yourself, or not having an inner adult you can count on.

### Related Clinical Work

This framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice. Later revisions also compare notes with other approaches, like schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy, spiritually integrated psychotherapy and so on. Those don't even agree with each other on everything! I borrow particular distinctions and practices rather than presenting the whole synthesis as their consensus or claiming that their research validates it as a package.
